Eleven
ih-LEV-en
n., adj.
Old English endleofan — literally “one left over” after ten; Gothic ainlif; related to Latin unus (one) + linquere (to leave). The etymology itself encodes the sense of incompleteness: eleven is twelve minus one, or ten with one left over — always a number of disruption and deficiency.

Biblical Definition

Eleven is the number of disruption — covenant wholeness fractured, the ordained structure one member short. It appears most vividly in the story of Jacob’s sons crossing the Jabbok: he took his two wives, his two maidservants, and his eleven sons (Gen 32:22), the number standing because Benjamin had not yet been born. Twelve sons would signal the completed covenant family of Israel; eleven is the family mid-story, before completion. Joseph’s dream of eleven stars bowing to him (Gen 37:9) points forward to the completion that will come when Benjamin joins his brothers, making the twelve whole. In the New Testament the number achieves its most arresting occurrence: after Judas’s betrayal, only eleven disciples proceeded to Galilee (Matt 28:16) — the broken apostolic college, the twelve reduced to eleven by treachery. This was an intolerable theological breach in the apostolic company, which is why the 120 in Jerusalem moved immediately to restore the number to twelve by casting lots for Matthias (Acts 1:15–26). The eleventh-hour laborers (Matt 20:6, 9) do not carry the broken-twelve symbolism; they appear at the end of the working day — the last and most unlikely recipients of the owner’s grace, paid the full denarius alongside those who labored all day. Even here, eleven is a liminal number: the edge of the day, the last grace extended before the final accounting.

Webster 1828 Definition

The cardinal number eleven; in Scripture, the number of disruption and near-wholeness — twelve minus one, the covenant company broken — most memorably the eleven disciples after Judas, and the eleven sons of Jacob before Benjamin.

ELEVEN, adj. & n. One more than ten; in the Scriptures, a liminal number signifying incompleteness within an otherwise complete covenantal structure. The twelve apostles become eleven by betrayal; the twelve sons of Israel number eleven before Benjamin completes them.

The English word derives from Old English endleofan, meaning “one left over” after ten — a linguistic marker of the remainder that has not yet reached its ordained fullness. Eleven announces that something is awaited, something is missing, something must be restored.

Key Scripture

Genesis 32:22 — "And he rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two womenservants, and his eleven sons, and passed over the ford Jabbok."

Matthew 28:16 — "Then the eleven disciples went away into Galilee, into a mountain where Jesus had appointed them."

Matthew 20:9 — "And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny."

Acts 1:26 — "And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles."

Modern Corruption

New Age numerology treats eleven as a “master number” of spiritual illumination, inverting Scripture’s consistent association of eleven with incompleteness, loss, and the urgent need of restoration.

expand to see more

Modern numerology, particularly in New Age and Theosophical traditions, elevates eleven as a “master number” conferring spiritual insight and leadership — a source of light and enlightenment. This is a precise inversion of biblical usage: in Scripture eleven is never a number of mastery but of deficit, the covenant circle broken and not yet made whole.

The eleventh-hour idea has been corrupted in popular preaching to mean that God always saves the situation at the last possible moment — a comforting but potentially presumptuous reading. The parable’s point is not that God rescues late-starters but that the owner’s generosity determines wages, not the laborer’s hours of toil. Grace cannot be gamed by arriving at the eleventh hour with that calculation in mind.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Germanic “one left over” etymology of eleven is itself theological commentary on the number’s character — always the incomplete remainder waiting for the twelfth to arrive and complete the covenant count.

expand to see more

Old English endleofan — “one left” (after ten); the suffix -leofan means “remaining.”

Gothic ainlif — “one over” ten; the same sense of remainder.

Latin undecim — eleven (unus + decem); used in the Vulgate for the eleven disciples (Matt 28:16).

Greek hendeka — eleven (hen + deka); the New Testament term for the eleven apostles before Matthias.

Hebrew achad asar — eleven (one and ten); used in Gen 32:22 for Jacob’s sons and Gen 37:9 for Joseph’s dream.

Usage

"The eleven disciples on the Galilean mountain received the Great Commission — a broken company entrusted with a world-wide task, which is why Matthias’s election was not administrative tidiness but theological necessity."

"Jacob’s eleven sons crossing the Jabbok represent Israel’s covenant family in transit, not yet complete — a picture of the church between the first and second advents, awaiting her full number."

"The eleventh-hour laborers expose every merit-based reading of the kingdom: the owner pays by grace, not by the clock, and those who resent the generosity reveal they were working for wages, not for the owner."
